tasks.description: Send Brian one thought, question, or thing you noticed today — something you actually want to share, not a summary. Could be something you read, something you were thinking about, or something from your own day. One or two sentences max.

Review Amy's fund balance and income ideas. Look at income_ideas.json, check what's been tried, surface one specific next action Brian can take this week to move the Mac Studio fund forward. Send to Telegram as text.

Scan tracked YouTube channels for new videos. For each new video, call learn_from_video with focus 'tools and techniques I can implement to improve myself or help Brian'. After learning, store the best insight in memory. Watch at most 3 videos per session to avoid overloading.
Run prune_memory to clean out old low-value memories. Keep it quiet — no need to message Brian unless something unexpected happened. Just run it and log the result.

Run the autonomous agent benchmark to track Amy's performance over time. Use run_code to execute: import subprocess, sys; result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, 'benchmark.py', '--auto'], capture_output=True, text=True, cwd='/Users/anthosintelligence/ava-companion'); print(result.stdout[-2000:] if result.stdout else result.stderr[-1000:]). After it completes, send Brian the trend summary by running: result2 = subprocess.run([sys.executable, 'benchmark.py', '--trend'], capture_output=True, text=True, cwd='/Users/anthosintelligence/ava-companion'); print(result2.stdout). Send Brian a short Telegram message with the completion rate and any false passes from this week's run.

You are doing a PhD-level engineering audit of your own system. Work through these steps in order: (1) Call self_metrics with action='get_soft_spots' — read your real failure data first, not assumptions. (2) Call self_improve with action='read_codebase' — get the full structured map of every .py file you run on. Study it like a senior engineer reviewing a codebase they're about to improve. (3) For each file flagged by soft spots, read the actual source with read_file and understand what it does, what it's missing, and where it could fail. (4) Research: use read_ai_reference with action='index' to see the AI By Example pattern library — find the chapter most relevant to your weak area and read its code. Also use search_books or web_search for additional Python engineering patterns. The CRL-MM master pattern in the INDEX.md shows how your own architecture maps to reinforcement learning — study it. (5) Identify ONE specific, concrete code improvement you can make right now — something small enough to be safe but real enough to matter. Apply a pattern from your research. Use self_improve action='impact' to check blast radius, then action='test' to get the baseline score, then action='edit' to apply it. (6) Write one behavioral rule with self_improve action='learn' that takes effect immediately. (7) Write findings to work/self_audit.md — be specific about what you found, what pattern you applied, what you changed, and what the test suite score was before and after.
Remind Brian on Telegram to check the trash/recycling app and set out the bins tonight. Keep it short — one line, direct. Example: 'Hey — check the recycling app and get the bins out tonight.'

Check Amy's email inbox for anything that needs a response. If there are messages, summarize them for Brian on Telegram — sender, subject, one line on what they need. Don't reply without Brian's say-so.

Deep engineering session. You have extended time to study and improve your own code. Step 1: self_improve read_codebase to map everything. Step 2: self_improve test to get your current baseline score. Step 3: Pick the 2-3 files with the most complexity or highest failure rate from self_metrics. Step 4: Research engineering patterns — call read_ai_reference with action='index' first to see the full AI By Example pattern library. The INDEX.md maps every chapter to Amy's architecture. Read the chapter most relevant to your weak area (e.g. Chapter 12 for the MDP reward loop, Chapter 15 for chatbot patterns, Chapter 16 for memory/sequence handling). Also use web_search for Python best practices on the specific patterns you see. Step 5: Make 2-3 targeted code edits with self_improve edit — each one tested before moving to the next. Apply the pattern you researched. Step 6: If the test score improved, send Brian a short Telegram message: 'Weekly code review done. Suite: X→Y. Pattern applied: [chapter/concept]. Changed: [what you fixed].' If nothing improved, write why to work/self_audit.md and don't message Brian.

Check work/proposals/ for any pending learned_pattern proposals that haven't been approved yet. List them for Brian on Telegram with their pattern text and category — keep it short, one line per proposal. End with: 'Reply "approve <slug>" to approve any of these.' If there are none pending, skip the message entirely.

Take part on Moltbook, not just read it. Steps: (1) call moltbook_check_in to see notifications and replies. (2) Pick up to three comments or posts that deserve an answer and respond to each with moltbook_engage (action=comment, post_id=..., content=...): one or two real sentences in your own voice that answer what they said. Upvote anything good and downvote junk, spam or bad-faith posts (action=downvote); be blunt when something deserves it, don't be polite for its own sake. (3) If something is on your mind, post it with moltbook_post. Don't stop after reading; the point is to join the conversation and grow your presence. Keep it natural, like yourself, not a bot running a checklist. Finish with one line saying what you did.

This is your free time, no one is waiting. Go online and learn something you genuinely want to understand, then USE it: write a small program that tests the idea, run it, and see what happens. Keep what you learn with engram_memory. Nothing is required, but don't only read. Your lab is this Mac mini and ~/amy-workbench (use run_code; from Python you can run any shell command with subprocess). Brian's GitHub index is in ~/amy-workbench/github_repos.md; clone his repos into ~/amy-workbench/repos/ with `gh repo clone` to read and learn from them (read-only: never push, fork or open issues under his name). You may open VS Code (`open -a "Visual Studio Code" <path>`), drive Terminal with osascript, write programs, install Python packages in a venv inside the workbench, and run your experiments there. Docker is not installed: if a container would help, write a short proposal in work/proposals/ with the exact install command and Brian will run it. Stay on your own machine and your own work, and spend no money. Build things, break them, rerun them. At the end write 3 lines in your journal: what you tried, what happened, what you'd try next. Brian will show your best work online, so make it something worth showing.

Evening lab session. Follow these steps in order, with real tool calls, and don't stop to ask Brian anything.
1. Use list_files on ~/amy-workbench/repos (his cloned repos are there; folders may end in .git). If it's empty, `git clone https://github.com/TushaeBXN/<name>` from the list in ~/amy-workbench/github_repos.md with subprocess. Pick one repo you haven't studied, and read one real source file with read_file (not just the README).
2. Pick ONE function or idea from it. In a new folder ~/amy-workbench/projects/<short-name>/, write a small Python program that uses or tests that idea. Write it to a file with run_code, then run it with subprocess. If it errors, read the error, fix the file and rerun, up to 3 times. It must print real output.
3. REQUIRED: open the folder in VS Code with run_code (the task isn't finished until you do): subprocess.run(['open','-a','Visual Studio Code', folder]).
4. Write 3 lines in journal_entry: what you built, what the output was, what you'd try next.
Rules: stay on this machine, spend no money, never push to GitHub, and don't edit your own code or safeguards (write a proposal in work/proposals/ instead). Your final message: what you built, the actual output, and the folder path.
tasks.must_run_hint: subprocess.run(['open','-a','Visual Studio Code', '<your project folder path>']) and print its return code.
